procedural_history.originating_court: Election Petition No. 1 of 1968 was originally filed in the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The appeal challenges the judgment and order dated March 27, 1970, of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench, which dismissed the Election Petition No. 1 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dismissed the election petition. The High Court concluded that the appellant had not discharged the burden of proving that the statements made during the election campaign were false and believed to be false by the returned candidate, speakers, and the editor. The High Court also did not agree with the submission that the respondent's election expenses exceeded the prescribed limit, as the petrol purchased was not proven to be solely for election purposes.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Manoj Lal, approached the Supreme Court by way of an appeal under s. 116-A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, challenging the High Court's dismissal of his election petition.

directions: The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned statements, relating to a pending criminal complaint for embezzlement against the appellant, constituted a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

facts: During an election campaign, statements were made at a public meeting and published in a weekly, referring to the appellant as a corrupt candidate who had misappropriated money.
A criminal complaint for embezzlement had been filed against the appellant in 1965, years before the election in question.
This criminal complaint was still pending in court at the time the statements were made.
The appellant himself admitted under oath that a complaint for embezzlement had been filed against him.
law: Under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for a statement to be a corrupt practice, it must be proven to be false, and the person making it must either believe it to be false or not believe it to be true.
The Court cited the precedent of *Sheopalsingh v. Rampratap*, which holds that even if a statement is false, the person making it is protected if it was made in good faith (bona fide).
application: The Court reasoned that the existence of a pending criminal complaint for embezzlement against the appellant provided a valid basis for the respondent and the speakers to believe the statements were true.
The complaint was filed in 1965, long before the election was even contemplated, which suggested it was not a fabrication for the election.
Given the pending criminal case, the appellant failed to prove the crucial element that the respondent and others made the statements believing them to be false or not believing them to be true.
The Court held that the complaint and the order framing the charge in the criminal case were relevant and admissible evidence in this matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that the statements did not constitute a corrupt practice under Section 123(4). The appellant failed to prove that the statements were made with the belief that they were false or without a belief in their truth, especially since they related to a pending criminal complaint for embezzlement against him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the criminal complaint filed against the appellant and the order framing the charge in those proceedings were admissible in evidence.

facts: A criminal complaint for embezzlement had been filed against the appellant.
A charge was framed against the appellant in those criminal proceedings.
The appellant himself admitted on oath, as a witness, that the complaint had been filed against him.
law: The Court noted that the appellant's counsel failed to cite any provision of law that would render the criminal complaint or the order framing the charge inadmissible as evidence in the present proceedings.
application: The Court found that the appellant's own admission that a complaint was filed against him could not be ignored.
Given the appellant's admission and the absence of any law making them inadmissible, the Court determined that the complaint and the charge were relevant to the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the criminal complaint and the order framing the charge were relevant and admissible in evidence, as there was no provision of law making them inadmissible, and the appellant himself had admitted to the existence of the complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the impugned statements, relating to a pending criminal complaint for embezzlement against the appellant, constituted a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
appellant_arguments: The statements made at the meeting and published in 'Ranchandi' were false.
The respondent and his agents either believed the statements to be false or did not believe them to be true at the time they were made.

The appellant argued that if the court ignored the criminal court's order and considered his denial of embezzlement, the statements must be held to be false and to meet the criteria for a corrupt practice.
respondent_arguments: The appellant failed to discharge the heavy burden of proof under Section 123(4), which requires proving not only that the statement was false, but also that the publisher believed it to be false or did not believe it to be true.
The impugned statements were not based on mere suspicion or conjecture but had a positive basis: the criminal complaint for embezzlement filed against the appellant, which was a well-known fact.
The subsequent framing of a charge on the same material demonstrated that the statements were bona fide and prima facie correct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the criminal complaint filed against the appellant and the order framing the charge in those proceedings were admissible in evidence.
appellant_arguments: The order of the criminal court framing the charge and the complaint itself are inadmissible in the present proceedings.
The charge was framed after the statements were made, so it cannot be considered when determining if the statements were believed to be true at the time of publication.
The appellant's counsel failed to cite any provision of law that would render the documents inadmissible.
respondent_arguments: The criminal complaint and the order framing the charge were admissible evidence.
The appellant himself admitted under oath that the complaint was filed and a charge was framed, and this admission cannot be ignored.
This evidence was relevant to show that the statements made against the appellant had a factual basis.

cases.case_name: Dr. Jagjit Singh v. Giani Kartar Singh
cases.principle: Under s. 123(4) of the Act, there is a heavy burden on the petitioner to prove that an impugned statement of fact is not only false, but also that the person publishing it either believed it to be false or did not believe it to be true.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish a corrupt practice under section 123(4) of the Act, the petitioner bears a heavy burden to prove two essential ingredients: first, that the impugned statement of fact is false, and second, that the candidate or their agent who published the statement either believed it to be false or did not believe it to be true.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the appellant failed to meet the stringent requirements of a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The existence of a criminal complaint for embezzlement against the appellant provided a sufficient factual basis for the respondent's statements. Consequently, the appellant could not discharge the heavy burden of proving not only that the statements were false, but also the crucial ingredient that the respondent and his agents either believed the statements to be false or did not believe them to be true at the time they were made.
legal_tests_applied: To establish a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the petitioner bears a 'very heavy burden' to prove two vital ingredients: first, that the impugned statement of fact is false, and second, that the person publishing the statement either believed it to be false or did not believe it to be true.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to discharge the heavy onus of showing that the offending statements of fact were false.

The appellant provided absolutely no material on the record to prove the most vital ingredient of Section 123(4): that the respondent and his agents publishing the statements either believed them to be false or did not believe them to be true.
The appellant's challenge failed because the statements relating to him were not founded on mere suspicion or pure conjecture, but on the existing criminal complaint.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's statements had a factual basis, as they related to a criminal complaint for embezzlement that had been filed against the appellant.

The existence of this complaint demonstrated that the statements were not the result of mere suspicion, conjecture, or guess, which in turn meant the appellant could not prove the respondent's bad faith.

The High Court's reasoning, which this Court found 'unexceptionable', was that the existence of the complaint was enough material to show the appellant had not discharged his burden of proof under the statute.
